Mutant Game

By: Anna-Maria van Niekerk | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Mulit-million rand prices for colour and horn variant game belie an intensive ranching industry that threatens ecological devastation

Summary:
The practice of intensive wildlife breeding for colour and horn length variation threatens extensive game ranching practices and the last remaining wilderness areas as more and more farmers buy into what seems on the surface to be an extremely lucrative industry. Auctioned for millions and tens of millions of rands, the increasing availability of colour variant game seems to indicate a growing market for exotic wildlife -- but we investigate a sobering claim that there is in fact NO market for hunting this game. Neither meat nor trophy hunters' associations support the proliferation of these animals, and they have said they will not be the ones to hunt them. So where is the market? Who are these animals being bred for? At least some scientists feel that the exorbitant auction prices that these animals have fetched point to a dangerous pyramid that may collapse at some point, but not before the intensive breeding practices have destroyed ecosystems and wilderness areas.

Further information:
In former protection areas on google earth one can now see how farmers that once supported extensive farming practices now intensively farm game in small camps where the animals are treated exactly like cattle or sheep -- they are fed artificially through mineral licks and supplement-enriched pellets. In striving to keep their small camps free from pests and parasites, game farmers create sterile zones around these highly electrified camps. Electric fencing begins flat on the ground so rare small animals are electrocuted as they try to enter.

In the last fiver years that the practice has escalated exponentially, there has been active disinvestment by even crop and cattle farmers to use their land for intensive game breeding.

Since 1991 when the private ownership of game became legal in South Africa, game farmers have made significant contributions to ecological convervation. Intensive breeding is setting back these gains. It's cheaper to keep animals in small cams and guarantee their meat quality through feeding -- except no-one wants to hunt these expensive game...so the industry has conflated two practices (game meat cultivation & colour variant breeding) that will see even small farmers who have invested in intensive camps, lose out.

The only winners seem to the be investors who sell variant game for millions that escalate at each auction.

The fact that the auctioning of game occurs largely on a cash basis raises questions about the taxation and money laundering.

The fact that intensive colour variant breeding is unregulated doesn't mean that it is legal -- in harming the environment, the practice inherently breaks the Constitution as well as the National Environmental Management Act. It also goes against what KingIII on Corporate Governance calls the "Triple Bottom Line" directive, which says that any business should weight people's well-being against the value generated and the environmental impact of the activity.

We will investigation how colour variant breeding is potentially far more malevolent that previously thought. Buyers like Cyril Ramaphosa and other elite financiers argue that they support conservation, but in truth, these animals can never be released among pure herds again, as they are genetically weakened and weakened by the fact that they've been habituated, fed artificially and medicated when ill.



Extra Budget Items:
Recce of Limpopo and NorthWest areas where we have received information of intensive breeding. Also attendance at a conference in Kimberley of conservation scientists.

Press Release:


Mutant Game
A chocolate springbok for R2.4-million or a white-flanked impala for R1.2-million? Breeding colour variants of indigenous buck is big business for industry and proving to be highly lucrative compared to traditional game farming. Auctioned for tens of millions, the increasing availability of colour-variant game seems to indicate a growing market for unusual wildlife. But these animals are hardly bred for hunting trophies or meat. Could selective breeding practices be detrimental to sensitive ecosystems, biodiversity and conservation as a whole? Carte Blanche investigates.


Script:


BREEDING SCRIPT
Around South Africa their numbers are sky-rocketing. Strange creatures hardly seen in recent times on African plains — white springbuck. Golden Wildebeest. Black impala. Golden oryx. Saddleback blesbuck. They sell for absolute fortunes.
JOHN LINK: A black impala that costs R2-million. A golden wildebeest sets you back R5- million. A saddleback blesbok that fetches the handsome price of R30-million. These are the sorts of figures associated with the game breeding industry. But the question is how are these prices arrived at? Who decides on them? Or aren’t we just dealing with a false economy?
Last year billionaire Johann Rupert paid R40-million for a tuberculosis-free buffalo with unusually long horns. Average buffalos sell for up to a million rand. A kudu, at most R60,000 was bought for almost R10-million a few months ago.
The buyers claimed they bought good genetics to restore what hunting has destroyed.
But since the 90s selective breeding is also pursued for colour and coat variation —
and they too sell at inflated prices.
ELLALIEN MALAN: Ek dink ons almal partykeer al so ‘n gedagte gegee aan die storie en dan dink jy ‘joe nee hoe kan dit aanhou?’
WIAN VAN DER LINDE: this is the best opportunity to make an income per hectare in South Africa or Africa
Intensive, selective game breeding can look like this: smaller, electrified camps with feed and water laid on. Supplements, medicine and antibiotics are used. Predators are kept at bay.
Even where breeders have larger, semi-extensive camps, there’s controversy over the artificial manipulation of wildlife genetics, breeding game like cattle, and South Africa’s reputation around canned hunting.
Among breeders Piet du Toit from the Northwest Province is said to be the biggest. He hosts the annual auction with the most game and largest turnover in the country.
PIET DU TOIT: This is very high prices been paid, I think what’s happened in the colour variations in the beginning, the guys are buying a window opportunity for business.
Ellalien Malan and her children continue the breeding of colour variants that her father started many decades ago. She likens the high prices breeders are paying to what collectors are willing to pay for famous art works — a matter of personal taste.
ELLALIEN MALAN: In Afrikaans se mens ‘onbekend maak onbemind’, en dit is nogal baie waar wanneer dit by die kleur variasies kom.
JOHN LINK: Speak to the critics of the intensive farming of colour variant animals and you’ll hear Frankinstein freaks of nature...mutant species and In-breeding...but if anything this is a story about a very strong and very divergent views.
￼￼￼
￼ELLALIEN MALAN: As kind het my pa baie keer vir ‘n mens gese weet jy wat daai dier is eintlik mooi van lelikgeid....veral by ‘n blou willebees en ‘n dier soos ‘n tsessebe – dis definitief nie diere wat as jy hulle die eerste keer sien vir jou mooi is nie, maar hoe meer jy hulle sien, hoe meer mooi sien jy in hulle, want dan begin jy na die kleure kyk, jy begin kyk hulle reaksies, wat doen hulle in die veld, hoe tree hulle op, en dan begin hulle so ‘n klein plekkie in jou hart inkruip.
Organised hunting is sounding alarm bells because there is no consumer market for such expensive animals. Lizanne Nel is a conservation scientist for the organisation that represent hunters who shoot for the pot. Since hunting generates 70% of the wildlife industry’s income, Nel calls for regulation to protect Brand South Africa.
LIZANNE NEL: We’re not supporting hunting animals that have been captive bred or hunting of animals in small enclosures. So not only from a hunting perspective, but also from a tourism perspective, brand SA is what we’re selling to the international community out there is our extensive wildlife systems. If we have this disinvestment, what are we going to sell?
Nel’s research shows that intensive game farming is changing the landscape. Animal numbers may be conserved in intensive breeding camps, but biodiversity suffers. No-one knows how many fenced camps there are in an industry that has grown exponentially, unchecked, in the last decade. The Constitution demands conservation for the future.
LIZANNE NEL: Most of the Limpopo province, there’s huge areas where these concentrations of intensive breeding facilities are. In terms of our national conservation planning processes, these areas are still demarcated as wild areas, so in terms of expansion of our protected areas, it looks like they’re still available for expansion of our protected areas. But they’re not actually available any more. But because there’s no regulation of these activities, we don’t know what the extent of these intensive facilities.
But for Wian van der Linde and the breeders he represents, the mere suggestion of more regulation raises the hackles.
WIAN VAN DER LINDE: There’s too many permits and really some stuff doesn’t make sense...we apply to the same rules than national parks and provincial parks as a private entity...conservation is their primary focus at all cost and biodiversity. Our main focus is to make money financially and then conservation is the outcome.
JOHN WEBB: When you consider some of the prices being paid for these animals, do you think that that process is being manipulated at the auctions at all?
ELLALIEN MALAN: Dis maar mense wat bymekaarkom om spesifiek veilings te hou sodat hulle genoeg en voldoende diere het om ‘n goeie veiling te kan aanbied... daardie groepe is eintlik baie simpatiek teenoor mekaar, want jy weet as jy een dier op ‘n veiling goed verkoop dan is die kanse ook goed dat dit verder in die jaar baie goed sal gaan.
WIAN VAN DER LINDE: It’s a cash industry, no bank will give you finance to buy it, so there can’t be a bubble or a false economy. At this moment yes the breeders are determining the price because there is not an end user — at this moment the breeder is the end user.
￼The Professional Hunter’s Association’s Adri Kitshoff says no hunter will buy an animal worth millions. They usually hunt for a few thousand rands a head...and before a fair hunt becomes possible, intensively bred game has to be released and adjust to large areas.
ADRI KITSHOFF: There is clear legislation where an animal has been in a intensive area where it has been supplemented completely, the feeding the water everything is been supplemented by the land owner and it can’t be hunted. If an animal has been released into an extensive wildlife system where it can fend for itself that is legal to hunt an animal there.
JOHN LINK: Rubin Els, manager of Thaba Tholo, a 36ha game farm in Limpopo Province acknowledges the criticism agains the industry, but he says that much of it is unfounded.
Thaba Tholo is one of the largest of just over 11,000 game farms in the country — with intensive, well-fenced breeding camps and extensive spaces for hunting. They say colour variants make up about 10% of herds and help fund expansion.
RUBIN ELS: it’s elevated all the species and made people maybe realize to say ‘listen, let me not just shoot everything game has a real value now. And to a large degree the colour variants sort of put the emphasis on normal plains game; it won’t last forever, but for now it’s a very good platform.
Rubin dreams of repopulating Africa with all species lost to humans, but the breeders say “unfenced plains” is a romantic notion that hasn’t helped African conservation.
WIAN VAN DER LINDE: There is a saying I know people don’t like it, but that’s the truth – “if it pays, it stays”.
JOHN WEBB: It’ll be like any commodity on the stock exchange...and what you’re saying is that there will be at some point equilibrium?
RUBIN ELS: There will be equilibrium and the equilibrium people say ‘what are realistic prices’, ‘what should bottom-line price for a sable antelope be?’ And my views are hunting value...remember that most of the game farms in our country is situated on very marginal land; when I say marginal, not suitable for crop farming or even cattle farming.
Genetics Professor Paulette Bloomer warns that the scientific jury is still out on the long-term consequences of intensive breeding for the individual variants and for entire herds with variants mixed in.
PAULETTE BLOOMER: the research that we’re doing is not to prove the farmers or the breeders wrong, it’s to get to the underlying genetic basis of the colour determination so that they can also adjust their breeding practices according to that.
Government’s Department of Environmental Affairs wants the game ranching industry to sit down with hunters and based on good science, determine how regulation must work.
PAULETTE BLOOMER: Unfortunately a lot of people assume that it’s really simplistic and that it’s only a single genetic trait that is involved, but ... there are several ...what we call genetic loci, so different places that actually control how these inheritance patterns work.
And so, for example, in albino animals it is well known that there is deafness that segregates with that, so we need to find out what some of those potential other traits are that are passed on at the same time as some of these colour traits.
JOHN LINK: While the future appears a little bit uncertain it seems what’s needed now is a national dialogue to ensure the safety and wellbeing of these creatures.
LIZANNE NEL: The concern is at some point if the demand is satisfied, what are we going to do with all of these animals that we have in these small camps? We wouldn’t like to see those animals being made available to the hunting market because that’s going to tarnish our reputation as a responsible hunting industry.
PAULETTE BLOOMER: here’s a lot of concern internationally about what is happening in South Africa.
JOHN WEBB: Concerned internationally that some organizations won’t even classify some of these colour variants?
PAULETTE BLOOMER: Yes, and there’s the IUCN who’s got a specialist group on conservation and genetics and they’ve got the antelope specialists group and they have written a position statement on this – so they are very concerned about this.
PIET DU TOIT: You will see prices rising in the next ten years, big – time... but there will be some species, if the numbers is too much they will go sideways. The story that the pendulum will come back to the classics again...pure breeding with the Kudu and the Impala will come back and people will rather shoot a clean Impala than a black impala but there will be place for both of them ...
RUBIN ELS: Our business is game farming. The byproduct of what we do is actually nature conservation, but nature conservation is not our business...
WIAN VAN DER LINDE: We need to sit around a table we need to address it, there is enough space and there is willingness from our side to engage...

And so, for example, in albino animals it is well known that there is deafness that segregates with that, so we need to find out what some of those potential other traits are that are passed on at the same time as some of these colour traits. JOHN LINK: While the future appears a little bit uncertain it seems what’s needed now is a national dialogue to ensure the safety and wellbeing of these creatures. LIZANNE NEL: The concern is at some point if the demand is satisfied, what are we going to do with all of these animals that we have in these small camps? We wouldn’t like to see those animals being made available to the hunting market because that’s going to tarnish our reputation as a responsible hunting industry. PAULETTE BLOOMER: here’s a lot of concern internationally about what is happening in South Africa. JOHN WEBB: Concerned internationally that some organizations won’t even classify some of these colour variants? PAULETTE BLOOMER: Yes, and there’s the IUCN who’s got a specialist group on conservation and genetics and they’ve got the antelope specialists group and they have written a position statement on this – so they are very concerned about this. PIET DU TOIT: You will see prices rising in the next ten years, big – time... but there will be some species, if the numbers is too much they will go sideways. The story that the pendulum will come back to the classics again...pure breeding with the Kudu and the Impala will come back and people will rather shoot a clean Impala than a black impala but there will be place for both of them ... RUBIN ELS: Our business is game farming. The byproduct of what we do is actually nature conservation, but nature conservation is not our business... WIAN VAN DER LINDE: We need to sit around a table we need to address it, there is enough space and there is willingness from our side to engage...

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Mulit-million rand prices for colour and horn variant game belie an intensive ranching industry that threatens ecological devastation
metadata.Summary: The practice of intensive wildlife breeding for colour and horn length variation threatens extensive game ranching practices and the last remaining wilderness areas as more and more farmers buy into what seems on the surface to be an extremely lucrative industry. Auctioned for millions and tens of millions of rands, the increasing availability of colour variant game seems to indicate a growing market for exotic wildlife -- but we investigate a sobering claim that there is in fact NO market for hunting this game. Neither meat nor trophy hunters' associations support the proliferation of these animals, and they have said they will not be the ones to hunt them. So where is the market? Who are these animals being bred for? At least some scientists feel that the exorbitant auction prices that these animals have fetched point to a dangerous pyramid that may collapse at some point, but not before the intensive breeding practices have destroyed ecosystems and wilderness areas.
metadata.Further information: In former protection areas on google earth one can now see how farmers that once supported extensive farming practices now intensively farm game in small camps where the animals are treated exactly like cattle or sheep -- they are fed artificially through mineral licks and supplement-enriched pellets. In striving to keep their small camps free from pests and parasites, game farmers create sterile zones around these highly electrified camps. Electric fencing begins flat on the ground so rare small animals are electrocuted as they try to enter. In the last fiver years that the practice has escalated exponentially, there has been active disinvestment by even crop and cattle farmers to use their land for intensive game breeding. Since 1991 when the private ownership of game became legal in South Africa, game farmers have made significant contributions to ecological convervation. Intensive breeding is setting back these gains. It's cheaper to keep animals in small cams and guarantee their meat quality through feeding -- except no-one wants to hunt these expensive game...so the industry has conflated two practices (game meat cultivation & colour variant breeding) that will see even small farmers who have invested in intensive camps, lose out. The only winners seem to the be investors who sell variant game for millions that escalate at each auction. The fact that the auctioning of game occurs largely on a cash basis raises questions about the taxation and money laundering. The fact that intensive colour variant breeding is unregulated doesn't mean that it is legal -- in harming the environment, the practice inherently breaks the Constitution as well as the National Environmental Management Act. It also goes against what KingIII on Corporate Governance calls the "Triple Bottom Line" directive, which says that any business should weight people's well-being against the value generated and the environmental impact of the activity. We will investigation how colour variant breeding is potentially far more malevolent that previously thought. Buyers like Cyril Ramaphosa and other elite financiers argue that they support conservation, but in truth, these animals can never be released among pure herds again, as they are genetically weakened and weakened by the fact that they've been habituated, fed artificially and medicated when ill.
